name: Victor Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This is confidential. What is a normal day at the home-claims contact centre?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the team that takes the claim after the first answer has failed. A caller has a leak, and I compare the policy number, repair photograph and date before I authorise the next visit or explain a refusal. I have a two-year college diploma and a long memory for awkward policy wording. I use AI now and then to tidy a summary, but I check the evidence myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what does your pay support outside the centre?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Mei works paid hours at a school library. Our grown sons have their own flats, and we don't put their income in our household sums. I earn above the usual agent rate as a lead, and we have about ten months of expenses saved. The mortgage is still due each month, so the reserve is time to decide, not a second wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team a faster summary would be welcome if the claim file still shows the leak and the policy clause clearly. The first answer can be quick; a disputed refusal needs somebody to look again. I don't expect the lead desk to close for a little saved typing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid hours and Mei's library work should carry on. Ten months saved gives us room for a repair or a slow hiring month, though I will not call it retirement money. The AI draft I use sometimes does not decide whether a household gets a repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I'll keep the paid lead queue and check photographs against policy dates before signing a claims decision. I'll add a fixed share of each lead premium to our reserve while those shifts pay. If the plateau continues into its first year, I'll keep both habits rather than buy a new tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The mortgage gets paid from work in this picture, and I can still correct an error. I like a quiet file that ends with the repair booked, not another angry call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a photograph miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A dark patch can belong to last winter rather than yesterday's leak. The policy number is small, but the roof it refers to is not. I check the date and ask the caller what changed before I let a summary settle it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your sons help with a roof bill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They might offer, but they have rents of their own. Mei and I have a reserve for a real repair, and we'd check the invoice before drawing from it. I wouldn't promise the sons' wages to a mortgage lender.

I'd welcome a **faster summary** if a person can still reopen a disputed refusal.
think: I expect **lead hours** and Mei's library pay to continue.
I see ten months saved as **decision time**, not retirement income.

feel: **Calm** about wages and the ability to correct claim mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues that automatic claim checks can shorten a queue, but a household must be able to challenge a wrong refusal. I will join the union request for a paid human appeal rota with authority to reopen a file. The operator should publish which shifts are lost and which are moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first-contact agents may lose hours, and then my escalation team may shrink too. I am not afraid of a screen, but I only trust a new process after it fixes a real case. My occasional AI summaries do not make my higher lead wage secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll join the union group's written request for cut dates and paid claim-reopening authority. I'll keep handling paid escalation calls while the rota holds. If the operator posts an internal paid appeal shift, I'll inspect its written hours and authority before applying rather than treat an informal promise as a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a smaller paid team. I can help colleagues make a common request, but I cannot pay a mortgage with a title. A customer needs someone who can reopen a claim, not a nicer denial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as real appeal authority?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The appeal worker must be able to reopen the file, correct the evidence and send a repairer if the policy allows it. A button that only sends another letter is not authority. I want that power stated in the paid job description.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you test a new claims console?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, on a paid demonstration of the new console with an experienced colleague, using a closed case we later reversed. I would compare its decision to the correction we made. I am open to proof, but I won't leave my paid escalation rota for a demonstration alone.

I'd ask the operator to publish **shift cuts** and paid replacements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mei that 2028 thinking AI could read policy evidence and answer our claims before our team finishes the morning queue. Robots doing site visits follow around 2031. I would back a union demand for paid notice and a way for households to challenge an automatic refusal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the lead escalation desk could close in the first year after 2028. Ten months saved is a runway for a search, not the price of a new roof. Mei's library wage would not cover the mortgage and essentials alone for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I'll join the union's written demand for closure dates and paid claim appeals, and keep my paid escalation shifts while they exist. If the desk closes in the first year after 2028, I'll apply for a posted paid housing-survey assistant role only if written weekly hours and after-travel wages, together with Mei's actual pay, cover our mortgage and essentials. I'll take site duties only after a signed paid offer and safe instruction on the property.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though the reserve keeps me from taking the first advert I see. I have claim knowledge, not a surveyor's licence. A few years before robots reach site work is useful, but it isn't a whole future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check before a site visit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether I am measuring a wall with a trained worker or being asked to judge a structure I am not qualified to sign off. I would require safe instruction for the tasks before accepting paid site work. I can use the knowledge from claims, but I cannot pretend to be a qualified surveyor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no survey assistant role is posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd search other posted local paid work against our written mortgage budget while using only a bounded part of the existing reserve. I wouldn't treat a course advert as a vacancy. If paid claims shifts remain, I keep them until the desk actually closes.

I'd tell Mei **2028 AGI** reaches claim decisions before 2031 site robots.
think: I expect the **lead desk** could close quickly.
I know ten months saved and Mei's wage cannot replace the **mortgage-paying income** indefinitely.
do: Join the **union demand** for written closure dates and paid claim appeals in 2026.
After desk closure, apply for **posted paid survey assistance** only if written weekly hours and after-travel household wages cover mortgage/essentials.
Keep **paid claims** until closure; start site duties after signed offer and safe instruction; otherwise search budgeted paid jobs with bounded reserve.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected lead-income loss, while a ten-month cushion permits a careful search.
S2.quote: Ten months saved is a runway for a search, not the price of a new roof.
fieldNote: His **union request** seeks notice and paid human challenges to automatic claim refusals.
A survey assistant application follows **actual desk closure** and requires written weekly hours plus after-travel household mortgage coverage.
He is **not a licensed surveyor**; safe task instruction and a signed paid offer gate any site duties.

steps.text: Join union demand for written closure dates and paid claim appeals

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to test a real paid site route before 2031 thinking AI reaches the claims desk. A human appeal should still be able to reopen a wrong refusal. Robots around 2034 could change inspections later, so I won't sell the field as permanent shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could shadow a survey assistant on a paid shift and learn whether my knees and judgement suit the visits. A lead title inside the office still might go. I would keep earning while I find out, because ten months saved should not pay for a long experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I'll ask whether a posted paid survey-assistant opening offers one paid observation shift, and if it does I'll take it and check travel, safe duties and the written weekly hours. I'll keep taking paid claims calls and join colleagues asking the union for a paid human appeal rota. In the first year after 2031, if my lead hours are cut, I'll apply for a still-posted paid survey-assistant job only if its written weekly hours and after-travel household pay cover mortgage and essentials; I'll move only after a signed offer and safe instruction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the longer warning gives me time to see one real site. One paid site visit tells me more about my knees than a job title does. It might also show that this is the wrong route before I lose a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the observation shift is not offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid claims rota and check other posted local paid jobs against our written mortgage budget. I can ask for another field opening, but a waiting list isn't income. I won't pay for a course just to make an unposted job seem real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should hear the union's appeal request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The agents and claimants both should hear the answer. We would ask the operator to name the paid worker who can reopen a refusal and publish the appeal route. The union request belongs to the whole group, not just my team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our sons ten years lets us compare statements with bills, not declare that a pension will appear. I would be sixty-eight in 2036, and I might still need paid work. The site robots around 2039 do not give claim calls three extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ten-month reserve now is not a lifetime income, and Mei's library hours can change. I would like to stop the late lead shift while I can choose, but I won't set a retirement date from a story. I want the accounts and any actual income statement in front of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 Mei and I will check our mortgage, savings and actual income yearly and keep paid claims shifts while offered. I'll join the union's continuing request for a paid human claim appeal that can reopen wrong refusals. In the first year after 2036, if AGI ends those calls and we still need wages, I'll seek posted paid local work; if verified resources cover years of essential bills without my wage, I can decide to stop paid work rather than assume it now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A decade and a strong reserve make a planned choice possible, though I don't have the final numbers. A retirement date written in pencil cannot pay a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make stopping work a real choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Verified continuing income and savings that cover the mortgage, food and repairs for years, not just one winter. I don't know whether any pension payment applies to me, and I won't write one into the budget unseen. If the figures are short, I keep looking for paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the sons for money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Our grown sons have their own flats and lives. I'd rather show them a decision Mei and I can finance than ask them to finance it. I will not make a family promise from a guessed number.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the paid escalation desk could go before I understand another job. Written closure dates, a paid appeal route with reopening power and a real survey-assistant vacancy with safe instruction would help. A claim is not settled merely because the screen has stopped asking questions.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks a refusal after the customer has given up calling. Our files can look neat while someone still has water coming through the ceiling. That is the case I worry about.

headlineQuote: A claim is not settled merely because the screen has stopped asking questions.
portrait: At **fifty-eight**, Victor leads difficult home-claim calls using a two-year diploma and careful checks of policy evidence.
He has **higher lead pay**, ten months saved, a mortgage and a partner on school-library wages.
He uses AI summaries **occasionally**, but seeks union-backed paid reopening authority when automated claims threaten hours.
Fast AGI may close his **escalation desk**; a slower path allows conditional paid site observation without treating field work as permanent.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his paid escalation desk before he has a safe new wage.
whatWouldHelp: **Written closure dates**, paid claim appeals with reopening power and a real safe survey-assistant vacancy would help.
